Field studies of the Dolorous grass mouse (Akodon dolores) in its native Argentine lowland habitats have provided detailed life-history data under controlled laboratory conditions reflective of its active metabolic period. At a body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], which corresponds to the species' typical normothermic state, the gestation period in captive females was measured at 23 days [tg = 23 days]. This relatively short gestation, characteristic of many small-bodied murid rodents, is followed by the birth of altricial young. Newborn pups, entirely dependent on maternal care, display a wet weight at birth of only 2.6 grams [Wwb = 2.6 grams]. This low neonatal mass is consistent with the high litter sizes and rapid developmental rates observed across the genus Akodon, where a premium is placed on producing numerous offspring rather than investing heavily in each individual at parturition.

The early developmental trajectory of Akodon dolores is marked by a rapid progression through the pre-weaning phase. The nutritional dependence on the dam, characterized by intense suckling, culminates in the process of weaning at 26 days after birth [tx = 26 days after birth] when the body temperature is maintained at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This age at nutritional independence is relatively brief, allowing the female to redirect energetic resources toward subsequent reproductive events. Following the cessation of lactation, the young enter a sustained juvenile growth period that eventually leads to the onset of sexual maturation. Females attain puberty at 112 days from birth [tp = 112 days from birth], also measured under the standard thermal regime of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a timing that reflects a moderate delay before the initiation of gonadal activity.

Reproductive output in this species has been characterized in several captive colonies, revealing a pattern of moderate fecundity. Females typically produce litters of 3.9 pups [N_R_i = litters of 3.9 pups]. Under stable thermal conditions of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], females reproduce at a frequency of approximately one litter every 30 days [F_R_i = approximately one litter every 30 days], which translates into a moderate annual reproductive output. This strategy, combining a moderate litter size with the capacity for rapid successive litters, is relatively distinct among sympatric cricetid rodents and likely serves as an adaptation to unpredictable resource availability or high predation pressure in the seasonal grasslands they inhabit.

The ultimate body size achieved by adult Akodon dolores provides further insight into its life-history strategy. The maximum adult wet weight attained by reproductively mature individuals in the study population was 54 grams [Wwi = 54 grams]. This body mass is moderate for a member of the genus Akodon and is achieved through a period of sustained somatic growth after weaning. In comparison to other small mammals of similar size, the species appears to direct a substantial portion of its assimilated energy toward rapid growth to reach this adult mass, after which resources are largely partitioned toward the reproductive schedule described previously. The achievement of this ultimate mass is a prerequisite for successful breeding, as smaller individuals typically exhibit lower fecundity and reduced pup survival.

Longevity data collected from both field-captured and captive-maintained individuals indicate a relatively compressed lifespan typical of fast-lived small mammals. The maximum recorded lifespan for Akodon dolores is 4 years [am = 4 years] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This duration aligns with predictions from comparative analyses that link short lifespans to high extrinsic mortality rates and elevated reproductive effort. Within the context of its natural habitat, few individuals likely reach this upper age limit due to predation and seasonal environmental stressors. Such abbreviated longevity, among the shorter durations documented for Argentine akodontines, reflects the persistent mortality pressures inherent in its grassland environment, where the high energetic demands of frequent litters further constrain individual survival beyond a narrow reproductive window.
